questions.body: What is the Virtual DOM in React?
questions.keyPoints: A lightweight JavaScript object representation of the actual DOM tree.

options.text: A lightweight in-memory JavaScript object representation of the real DOM used by React to compute efficient DOM updates via diffing.
options.explanation: React maintains a virtual tree of plain JS objects describing what the UI should look like. On updates, it diffs the new virtual tree against the previous one (reconciliation) and applies minimal mutations to the real DOM.

options.text: A browser technology implemented in C++ alongside the WebKit engine.
options.explanation: Virtual DOM is a user-land JavaScript concept, not a native browser engine implementation.

options.text: A copy of the DOM stored in local storage for offline browsing.
options.explanation: It lives purely in JavaScript heap memory during runtime.

options.text: A direct alias for the browser's Shadow DOM specification.
options.explanation: Shadow DOM is a W3C standard for style scoping; Virtual DOM is React's internal diffing mechanism.

questions.body: Why does React require a unique `key` prop when rendering dynamic arrays of elements?
questions.keyPoints: Keys help React identify which items have changed, been added, or been removed during reconciliation.

options.text: To give elements a stable identity between renders, allowing React to track which items changed, moved, or were deleted during reconciliation.
options.explanation: Keys match virtual elements across renders. Without stable unique keys, reordering or inserting list items causes React to mutate DOM nodes inefficiently and corrupt component state.

options.text: To apply unique CSS styles to each list item automatically.
options.explanation: Keys are used by the reconciler and are not passed to CSS or DOM element attributes.

options.text: To allow elements to be searched using `document.getElementById`.
options.explanation: Keys are internal to React and do not become DOM element IDs.

options.text: To bind keyboard shortcut keys to list items.
options.explanation: Key prop is purely for list reconciliation identity.

questions.body: Why is using array index as a `key` prop (e.g., `key={index}`) considered an anti-pattern when list items can be reordered, inserted, or deleted?
questions.keyPoints: Indices change on insertions/deletions, causing React to associate internal component state with the wrong item.

options.text: When items are sorted, prepended, or removed, indices change, leading React to confuse item identities and attach component state or uncontrolled inputs to the wrong items.
options.explanation: If item 0 is deleted, item 1 becomes index 0. React believes the first component merely updated its props rather than having been replaced, causing visual bugs and state corruption in inputs.

options.text: Because numbers cannot be converted to valid React keys.
options.explanation: React accepts numbers and strings as keys.

options.text: It throws an immediate runtime exception in production builds.
options.explanation: React only outputs a console warning in development mode.

options.text: It disables all React hooks inside child components.
options.explanation: Hooks still execute, but their state may be associated with the wrong item.

questions.body: What does 'unidirectional data flow' mean in React?
questions.keyPoints: Data flows downwards from parent to child components via props.

options.text: State flows down the component hierarchy from parent to child via props; children communicate changes upwards by invoking callback functions passed by parents.
options.explanation: React enforces one-way data binding: parent components pass state down as props. To alter parent state, children invoke callbacks passed down as props.

options.text: Data flows automatically bidirectionally between any two sibling components.
options.explanation: React does not support automatic two-way data binding like legacy AngularJS.

options.text: Data can only travel from child components up to root components.
options.explanation: Data flows downward from parents to children.

options.text: HTTP requests can only be sent using the GET method.
options.explanation: Unidirectional data flow is an architecture pattern for UI state and props.

questions.body:
What does JSX code like `
Hello
` compile into in modern React?
questions.keyPoints: Compiles to jsx() or React.createElement() calls returning React elements.

options.text: Nested function calls to `jsx()` (or `React.createElement()`) that return plain JavaScript objects describing the element tree.
options.explanation: Compilers like Babel or SWC transform JSX tags into `jsx('div', { className: 'box', children: ... })` calls, which produce plain React Element objects.

options.text: Raw HTML strings injected via `innerHTML`.
options.explanation: React does not use innerHTML for standard component rendering.

options.text: Compiled WebAssembly bytecode.
options.explanation: JSX compiles to standard JavaScript.

options.text: Direct live DOM elements created via `document.createElement()` immediately.
options.explanation: JSX creates virtual element descriptors; the renderer converts them to DOM nodes during the commit phase.

questions.body: What was the primary goal of the React Fiber rewrite introduced in React 16?
questions.keyPoints: To enable incremental rendering and the ability to pause, abort, or prioritize rendering work.

options.text: To enable incremental rendering, allowing React to pause, resume, prioritize, and abort work chunks so heavy renders do not block the main browser thread.
options.explanation: The legacy Stack reconciler was synchronous and recursive. Fiber converted the call stack into a linked-list of fibers that can be paused to let the browser handle user input, enabling Concurrent features.

options.text: To rewrite the React runtime entirely in WebAssembly for raw execution speed.
options.explanation: Fiber is implemented in standard JavaScript.

options.text: To remove JSX syntax and enforce template files.
options.explanation: JSX was preserved completely.

options.text: To replace Redux with built-in database drivers.
options.explanation: Fiber is an internal reconciler architecture, not a state library.

questions.body: What is the difference between a Controlled component and an Uncontrolled component in React forms?
questions.keyPoints: Controlled component input value is driven by React state; uncontrolled component value is managed by the DOM itself.

options.text: In a controlled component, form input values are driven directly by React state via `value` and `onChange`; in an uncontrolled component, the DOM handles input state accessed via a `ref`.
options.explanation: Controlled components have React state as the 'single source of truth'. Uncontrolled components let the DOM maintain form state, which is queried on demand via `useRef()`.

options.text: Controlled components cannot use validation.
options.explanation: Controlled components make real-time validation trivial because state updates on every keystroke.

options.text: Uncontrolled components are forbidden in React 18+.
options.explanation: Both patterns are fully supported and valid.

options.text: Controlled components always submit form data via WebSockets.
options.explanation: Form submission mechanisms are independent of controlled state.

questions.body: Why do developers use `React.Fragment` (or `<>...</>`) when returning multiple elements from a component?
questions.keyPoints: Groups a list of children without adding an extra node to the real DOM.

options.text: To group multiple child elements together without adding an extra wrapper node (like an unnecessary `<div>`) to the DOM tree.
options.explanation: React components must return a single root element. `<React.Fragment>` fulfills this requirement without introducing redundant markup that could break Flexbox/Grid layouts.

options.text: To cache component renders in local storage.
options.explanation: Fragments have no caching behavior.

options.text: To enforce that all children render asynchronously.
options.explanation: Fragments are transparent wrappers in the virtual tree.

options.text: To enable Redux context access.
options.explanation: Fragments have nothing to do with Redux.

questions.body: What does `React.memo` do when wrapping a functional component?
questions.keyPoints: Memoizes the component, skipping re-renders if props have not shallowly changed.

options.text: It performs a shallow comparison of incoming props and skips re-rendering the component if props have not changed.
options.explanation: `React.memo` is a higher-order component. If its wrapped component renders the same result given the same props, React will skip rendering and reuse the last rendered result.

options.text: It deeply compares props recursively down through all nested objects.
options.explanation: By default, `React.memo` only performs a shallow comparison (`Object.is`). A custom comparison function can be passed as the second argument.

options.text: It caches all API network responses made inside the component.
options.explanation: It memoizes UI rendering, not HTTP requests.

options.text: It forces child components to re-render on every state change.
options.explanation: It is an optimization to prevent unnecessary re-renders.

questions.body: Why must React component rendering functions remain 'pure'?
questions.keyPoints: Same inputs produce same JSX, and no side effects during rendering phase.

options.text: Given the same props and state, they must return the same JSX without modifying external variables or triggering side effects during the render phase.
options.explanation: React can call component render functions multiple times, concurrently, or discard them before committing to the DOM. Side effects in render functions cause subtle bugs and inconsistent UI.

options.text: Pure functions execute 10 times faster in the V8 engine.
options.explanation: Purity is an architectural contract for predictability and concurrency, not a V8 engine flag.

options.text: Impure components cannot use JSX syntax.
options.explanation: Syntax is unaffected, but runtime behavior becomes buggy.

options.text: React throws a compile error if a function is impure.
options.explanation: Compilers cannot detect all forms of impurity at compile time.

questions.body: In React's architecture, what happens in the 'Render Phase' versus the 'Commit Phase'?
questions.keyPoints: Render phase calculates diffs (can be paused/restarted); Commit phase applies DOM changes synchronously.

options.text: Render phase calls component functions and computes changes (can be interrupted/aborted); Commit phase synchronously applies changes to the actual DOM and runs layout effects.
options.explanation: The render phase is purely computational (building fiber trees and diffing). The commit phase is where React actually mutates the DOM tree and invokes `useLayoutEffect` / `useEffect`.

options.text: Render phase paints pixels on the monitor; Commit phase parses JSX.
options.explanation: The browser handles monitor pixel painting after the commit phase.

options.text: Render phase is synchronous and irreversible; Commit phase can be paused.
options.explanation: The render phase is interruptible in Concurrent React; the commit phase is synchronous.

options.text: Commit phase only runs on the Node.js server.
options.explanation: The commit phase applies DOM mutations in the client browser (or native views in React Native).

questions.body: What lifecycle method or hook allows a class component to act as an Error Boundary in React?
questions.keyPoints: static getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch.

options.text: `static getDerivedStateFromError()` and `componentDidCatch()`
options.explanation: An Error Boundary is a class component that defines `getDerivedStateFromError` (to render fallback UI) and/or `componentDidCatch` (to log error info) to catch errors anywhere in its child tree.

options.text: `useErrorBoundary()` hook in React 18.
options.explanation: React does not yet have a native functional hook for error boundaries; class components are still required.

options.text: `window.onerror` handler.
options.explanation: `window.onerror` handles global JS errors, but cannot preserve React component tree state.

options.text: `try...catch` blocks around `<App />` in index.js.
options.explanation: `try...catch` cannot catch errors thrown inside asynchronous lifecycle/rendering methods of child components.

questions.subtopic: What Error Boundaries Do NOT Catch
questions.body: Which type of errors are NOT caught by React Error Boundaries?
questions.keyPoints: Event handlers, asynchronous callbacks, server-side rendering, errors in boundary itself.

options.text: Errors inside asynchronous code (e.g. `setTimeout`), event handlers (e.g. `onClick`), Server-Side Rendering, and errors in the boundary component itself.
options.explanation: Error boundaries catch errors during rendering, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors of child components. They do NOT catch errors in event handlers (use `try/catch`), async callbacks, or SSR.

options.text: Errors inside child component render functions.
options.explanation: Catching render errors in child components is the exact primary purpose of error boundaries.

options.text: Errors thrown inside `useEffect` callbacks.
options.explanation: Errors in `useEffect` propagate to the nearest Error Boundary.

options.text: Errors caused by invalid JSX syntax.
options.explanation: Syntax errors fail at build time before execution.

questions.body: What is the primary use case of `ReactDOM.createPortal(children, container)`?
questions.keyPoints: Renders children into a different DOM subtree outside parent container while preserving React context/event bubbling.

options.text: Rendering children into a different DOM node outside the parent component's DOM hierarchy (like modals, tooltips, or dropdowns) while preserving React event bubbling.
options.explanation: Portals allow rendering UI into `document.body` or other root nodes to break out of parent `overflow: hidden` or `z-index` stacking contexts, while remaining a child in the React virtual tree.

options.text: Routing between pages without changing browser URLs.
options.explanation: Portals are for DOM tree placement, not URL routing.

options.text: Streaming video frames into HTML5 Canvas.
options.explanation: Not related to video decoding or canvas.

options.text: Creating background Web Worker threads for React state.
options.explanation: Portals place DOM nodes in the main browser document.

questions.body: What is React's `SyntheticEvent` wrapper?
questions.keyPoints: A cross-browser wrapper around the browser's native event with the same interface.

options.text: A cross-browser wrapper around native browser events that provides consistent event properties across all browsers and delegates listeners at the root container.
options.explanation: React wraps native events in a `SyntheticEvent` to normalize cross-browser inconsistencies. Since React 17, event listeners are attached to the root container (`#root`) rather than `document`.

options.text: A library for generating mock events in unit tests only.
options.explanation: SyntheticEvent is the core event system in production React runtime.

options.text: An event system that runs completely off the main thread in a Service Worker.
options.explanation: It runs on the main JavaScript thread.

options.text: A mechanism that disallows calling `e.preventDefault()`.
options.explanation: `e.preventDefault()` works as expected on SyntheticEvents.

questions.body: Why does React `<StrictMode>` intentionally invoke component functions and effects twice in development mode?
questions.keyPoints: To detect side effects in the render phase and ensure cleanup functions are properly implemented.

options.text: To flush out impure side effects in render functions and ensure effects correctly implement setup and cleanup logic.
options.explanation: In development, React double-invokes render functions and mounts/unmounts/remounts components to help developers catch memory leaks, missing cleanup functions, and unexpected side effects.

options.text: Because development servers run at 30 FPS.
options.explanation: Frame rate is unrelated to React StrictMode.

options.text: It is an unintentional bug in React 18 that will be removed.
options.explanation: It is an intentional, documented feature designed for resilient Concurrent features.

options.text: It also executes twice in production builds for security.
options.explanation: Double-invocation occurs strictly in development builds; production is single-invocation.

questions.body: What component must wrap dynamic imports rendered via `React.lazy()`?
questions.keyPoints: React.Suspense with a fallback prop.

options.text: `<React.Suspense fallback={<Loading />}>`
options.explanation: `React.lazy()` takes a function that calls a dynamic `import()` and returns a component. It must be rendered inside a `<Suspense>` component that provides a fallback while the bundle loads.

options.text: `<ErrorBoundary>`
options.explanation: While an Error Boundary is good practice for failed network bundles, `<Suspense>` is mandatory.

options.text: `<React.Fragment>`
options.explanation: Fragment does not handle suspended asynchronous promises.

options.text: `<StrictMode>`
options.explanation: StrictMode does not manage asynchronous bundle loading states.

questions.body: What is a Higher-Order Component (HOC) in React?
questions.keyPoints: A function that takes a component and returns a new enhanced component.

options.text: A pure function that takes an existing component and returns a new enhanced component with added props or behavior.
options.explanation: An HOC (`const Enhanced = withAuth(MyComponent)`) is an advanced pattern in React for reusing component logic by wrapping components and passing transformed props.

options.text: A component that sits at the top level of the DOM tree (e.g. `<App />`).
options.explanation: That is the root component.

options.text: A component that renders directly to an HTML5 canvas.
options.explanation: HOCs operate on standard React components.

options.text: A class component that cannot use state.
options.explanation: HOCs frequently inject state and lifecycle handlers.

questions.body: What problem does the React Context API primarily solve?
questions.keyPoints: Prop drilling (passing props through intermediate components that don't need them).

options.text: Prop drilling, by providing a way to share values (themes, auth status, locale) to all components in a tree without manually passing props through every level.
options.explanation: Context is designed to share data that can be considered 'global' for a tree of React components, bypassing intermediate components that do not need the data.

options.text: Replacing all REST API backend endpoints.
options.explanation: Context is client-side state distribution, not backend networking.

options.text: Eliminating all component re-renders completely.
options.explanation: When context value changes, all consuming components re-render.

options.text: Compiling React into static HTML pages.
options.explanation: Context operates dynamically in both SSR and client runtime.

questions.body: In React, what does the special `props.children` property contain?
questions.keyPoints: The content and nested elements placed between a component's opening and closing JSX tags.

options.text: The content and nested elements placed between the opening and closing tags of a component in JSX.
options.explanation:
Composition via `props.children` allows components (like `

Content

`) to pass arbitrary JSX inside them without knowing their children in advance.

options.text: An array of child database records fetched from an API.
options.explanation: It refers to nested JSX children.

options.text: The internal private state variables of the component.
options.explanation: State is managed via `useState`, not `props.children`.

options.text: The DOM node coordinates of child elements.
options.explanation: Coordinates are read from DOM geometry APIs, not props.
